title: Twice-yearly lenacapavir for HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis: both phase 3 trials, reported as incidence rate ratios, with the randomised and the counterfactual comparisons kept apart
question: In the two phase 3 lenacapavir prevention trials, what is the incidence of HIV acquisition with lenacapavir relative to the randomised oral active control, and separately relative to the background incidence estimated in the screened population?
_prose_rule: Every text field is PROSE unless it is on the validator's numeric list. Prose may not restate a number the object holds structurally.
_sourcing_rule: Every MEASURED input carries the verbatim sentence it was read from. No measured input is stored that the staged sources do not carry, which is why this object has no person-years field. DERIVED transforms of stored values -- the log point and log standard error of a ratio -- are stored and are not claimed to appear in any source; an earlier wording said no figure at all was stored beyond the sources, which was false of those fields.
_estimand_rule: The estimand is an incidence rate over person-time. Events and participants are stored because they are published, and NOT in the shape of a table of participants with and without an event, so that no risk ratio can be computed from them.
completeness_statement: FULL BUILD: both phase 3 trials of this intervention are held and reported. Nothing was cited and dropped.

handbook.decision: REPORT each trial separately; compute NO pooled estimate
handbook.conformance: ONE reason is sufficient and it is arithmetic rather than judgement: PURPOSE 1's rate ratio is exactly zero, so it has no logarithm, and the generic inverse-variance method that sections 10.3.3 and 10.8 prescribe for combining rate ratios operates on log ratios. There is nothing to give it. Section 10.4.4 is cited for what it actually covers -- rare events in two-by-two data, where it recommends the Peto method and warns that adding a half to each cell 'usually has the undesirable effect of biasing study estimates towards no difference'. That warning is about CELLS and these are RATES, so it is cited as the nearest guidance rather than as governing; a reviewer objected to an earlier version that cited it as though it governed, and was right. A Peto odds-ratio synthesis on the participant counts IS computable and is not performed for two stated reasons: it would silently change the estimand from the rate ratio both trials published to an odds ratio on participants, and both trials allocated unequally, which is the condition 10.4.4 identifies as biasing that method. The population difference between the trials is recorded as clinical diversity under 10.10.1 and is NOT claimed to be independently sufficient -- an earlier version did claim that, which is stricter than the Handbook, since 10.10.3 treats declining to synthesise as a judgement about whether an average would mislead and random-effects models exist precisely to carry such diversity.

handbook.decision: REPORT each trial separately; compute NO pooled estimate, and never combine this with the randomised contrast
handbook.conformance: The comparator is not a randomised group. Section 3.2.3 distinguishes the kinds of comparison a review may make, and an estimate against an incidence modelled in a screened population is not the same quantity as a contrast between two randomised arms: it carries the assumptions of that model and none of the protection randomisation provides. The two are reported as separate outcomes for that reason. No synthesis across trials is computed here either, and the governing reason is the same arithmetic one as for the randomised contrast -- one trial's rate ratio is zero and the generic inverse-variance method of 10.3.3 and 10.8 has no log ratio to take. An earlier version invoked that reason here while citing only the comparison-definition and heterogeneity sections, which did not govern it.
